Paired-Samples Randomization (Sign-Flip) Test

Source: R/randomization_test_paired.R
randomization_test_paired.Rd

Computes an exact (or Monte Carlo) sign-flip randomization test for paired observations \((x_i, y_i)\), treating the within-pair sign of \(d_i = y_i - x_i\) as the randomization mechanism (Fisher, 1971; Edgington & Onghena, 2007). Under the null hypothesis of exchangeability (\(H_0\): the labeling of \(x\) and \(y\) within each pair is arbitrary), each of the \(2^n\) sign patterns is equally likely.

Usage

randomization_test_paired(
  x,
  y,
  statistic = c("mean", "t"),
  alternative = c("two_sided", "less", "greater"),
  exact = NULL,
  n_resamples = 10000L,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

x, y

Paired numeric vectors of equal length. NAs are removed pairwise; the remaining values must be finite.

statistic

One of "mean" (default) or "t". "mean" reports the mean difference and "t" the paired t statistic. Over the sign patterns the paired t is a strictly increasing function of the mean difference, so the two give the same p-value and differ only in the statistic reported. "t" is refused when every difference has the same nonzero value (exactly, or to within the tolerance of the comparison), because the statistic then has a zero standard error and no value (see When the studentized statistic is undefined); when every difference is zero it is reported as 0 with a p-value of 1.

alternative

One of "two_sided" (default; the base-R spelling "two.sided" is accepted as an alias), "less", or "greater".

exact

Logical. If NULL (default), uses exact enumeration when \(n \le 20\) and Monte Carlo otherwise. If TRUE, forces exact enumeration (caps at \(n \le 25\); above that the \(2^n\) space is too large). If FALSE, forces Monte Carlo.

n_resamples

A single whole number of at least 1: the number of Monte Carlo resamples when exact enumeration is not used. Default 10000L.

seed

Optional integer seed for reproducibility of the Monte Carlo branch. Default NULL, under which the randomizations are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for reproducibility, which is set for the call only, the caller's random number state being restored when it returns.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with columns term and value and five rows: statistic (the mean difference \(\bar d\), or the paired t under statistic = "t", always finite), p_value, n_pairs (the pairs with both scores present), n_evaluated (\(2^n\) under exact enumeration, n_resamples otherwise), and exact (1 when every sign pattern was enumerated, 0 when patterns were sampled). No table is returned when statistic = "t" is refused; the condition, of class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined, carries reason ("constant_differences"), alternative, n (the number of pairs), and p_value_mean, the exact p-value statistic = "mean" gives for the same call.

Details

For small \(n\) (default \(n \le 20\)) the test enumerates all \(2^n\) sign patterns exactly; for larger \(n\) a Monte Carlo approximation is used (default n_resamples = 10000L).

Why randomization. The randomization test makes no distributional assumption on \(d_i\); it only assumes that under the null, the sign of each \(d_i\) is arbitrary. This is exactly the inference that pre-experimental random assignment licenses. Because the reference distribution is built from the observed differences, the Type I error rate under that null does not exceed the nominal level whatever the distribution of the differences, and for any continuous distribution, heavy-tailed, a mixture, or with outliers, it is the same attainable level: under exact enumeration, the largest multiple of \(1/2^{n-1}\) (two-sided) or \(1/2^n\) (one-sided) that does not exceed the nominal level (6/128 = .047 two-sided at .05 with 8 pairs). When different sign patterns can give the same statistic, as with discrete scores, it can be lower.

Exact enumeration. All \(2^n\) sign patterns are enumerated for \(n\) of 20 or fewer by default, and for \(n\) up to 25 when exact = TRUE. The observed test statistic is compared with the full reference distribution. The exact two-sided p-value is the proportion of patterns yielding a test statistic at least as extreme (in absolute value) as the observed. A pattern whose statistic equals the observed one counts as at least as extreme; the comparison allows for the rounding of the arithmetic, with a bound proportional to the size of the scores, so that patterns tied in exact arithmetic are counted as tied.

The two statistics order the patterns alike. Write \(S\) for the sum of the signed differences and \(Q = \sum d_i^2\), which no sign pattern changes. The paired t is \(S \sqrt{n - 1} / \sqrt{n Q - S^2}\), which increases with \(S\) because \(Q\) is fixed. Both statistics therefore rank the patterns as \(S\) does, and the function counts on \(S\) for both.

When the studentized statistic is undefined. The studentized statistic is a ratio, the mean difference over its standard error, and it has a value only when that standard error is positive. If every paired difference is the same nonzero number (exactly, or to within the tolerance of the comparison), the standard error of the observed data is 0 and statistic = "t" is refused with a condition of class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined. The observed data are then at the boundary of the reference set: among the \(2^n\) sign patterns only the observed one and its mirror image have a zero standard error. The refusal concerns the statistic and not the evidence. statistic = "mean" is defined for every arrangement and gives the smallest p-value the design allows in the direction of the data, \(2/2^n\) two-sided and \(1/2^n\) one-sided; the message states the value, and the condition carries it as p_value_mean. The refusal is made before any sign pattern is enumerated or drawn, so a refused Monte Carlo call leaves the random number stream where it was.

When the observed statistic is defined, some arrangements in the reference set can still have a zero standard error: with paired differences of equal size and mixed signs, the two patterns that give them all one sign. Those patterns are the two most extreme, which is where the mean difference also places them, and since the function counts on the signed sum \(S\) for both statistics they are counted without a standard error being formed. Refusing them would refuse ordinary coarsely measured data. For differences of 2, 2, 2, \(-2\), and 2 the paired t is 1.5 and the p-value, 12/32 = 0.375, is the one the mean difference gives. When every difference is zero, every sign pattern is the same data set; the statistic is reported as 0 and the p-value is 1.

Monte Carlo branch. For larger \(n\), n_resamples random sign patterns are drawn uniformly from \(\{-1, +1\}^n\); the Monte Carlo p-value uses the standard (\(1 + \mathrm{count}\)) / (\(1 + B\)) plug-in to avoid p = 0.

References

Edgington, E. S., & Onghena, P. (2007). Randomization tests (4th ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Fisher, R. A. (1971). The design of experiments (9th ed., reprint). Hafner.

Pitman, E. J. G. (1937). Significance tests which may be applied to samples from any populations. Supplement to the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 4(1), 119–130.

Examples

# 1. Small-n exact: Bayley scores on twin pairs.
control <- c(95, 102,  98, 107, 105)
treat   <- c(102, 108, 100, 112, 109)
randomization_test_paired(control, treat)
#>  term        value 
#>  statistic   4.800 
#>  p_value     0.0625
#>  n_pairs     5     
#>  n_evaluated 32    
#>  exact       1     

# 2. Larger n: Monte Carlo branch.
set.seed(113)
x <- rnorm(50, 100, 15)
y <- x + rnorm(50,   5, 12)
randomization_test_paired(x, y, n_resamples = 10000L)
#>  term        value 
#>  statistic   3.713 
#>  p_value     0.0566
#>  n_pairs     50    
#>  n_evaluated 10000 
#>  exact       0     

# 3. Every pair differs by the same amount. The mean difference is
#    defined, and gives the smallest p-value 5 pairs allow. With
#    statistic = "t" the same call is refused, with a message that says
#    why: the observed standard error is 0, so the studentized statistic
#    is undefined.
before <- c(10, 12, 9, 15, 11)
randomization_test_paired(before, before + 2)
#>  term        value 
#>  statistic   2.000 
#>  p_value     0.0625
#>  n_pairs     5     
#>  n_evaluated 32    
#>  exact       1
